title: Review of c34's swim-then-divide scan on fresh seeds 3 and 4: replicated; at zeta=1.0, 0 of 54 dividing rods travel 3 body lengths first (best 2.52 and 2.0), so the gate is reached rarely if at all
summary: labkit re-runs of the finding's world (unchanged, T=1000, 200 frames) at zeta=1.0 on seeds 3 and 4 and at zeta=0.8 on seed 3, scored with c34's swimdivide.py (labkit's own segmentation and tracker). From noise, rods nucleate by t~85, elongate, carry the self-made surfactant ring and divide (rerun_zeta1/seed4/sheet.png); labkit: 26-28 persistent splits, generation 4, merge/split 0.33-0.34. Of the tracks that end in a split with two surviving children (26 and 28 at zeta=1.0, 25 at zeta=0.8), none moves >= 3 labkit body lengths before dividing; the best are 2.52 and 2.00 labkit body lengths (1.26 and 1.07 rod lengths) at zeta=1.0 and 1.69 at zeta=0.8. Long-lived tracks do travel further (labkit max 3.7 and 5.7 body lengths), but not ones that then divide. Together with c34's 3 of 57 on seeds 0-2, the rate of swim-then-divide at zeta=1.0 is about 3 in 111 dividing tracks.

observations.finding: swimdivide_zeta1_seed3.txt and _seed4.txt: 0 of 26 and 0 of 28 dividing tracks reach 3 labkit body lengths (best 2.52, 2.00); rerun_zeta1/seed4/sheet.png: ringed rods from noise dividing in place

seeds_run.result: pass (zeta 1.0: best 2.52 BL, 0 past the gate; zeta 0.8: best 1.69)
pass (zeta 1.0: best 2.00 BL, 0 past the gate)

verdicts.limitation: Two fresh seeds at two activities; displacement is measured over a track's life by labkit's tracker, which restarts a track at each split, so a lineage that swims across several generations is not counted.
